# Mixed advanced contest habits

At this level, a powerful tool is useful only after the mathematical model
has earned it. This contest tests whether you can choose that model without
being told the technique in the statement.

# Nineteen original problems

The contest contains nineteen self-contained packages, A--S. The seven new
problems M--S bring each technical topic in sections 43--49 to two main
problems across the section-50 set. Together with section 42's coverage of
section 41, this closes the gap between the two mixed contests.

| Problem | Title |
|---|---|
| A | DAG Grundy |
| B | General CRT |
| C | Fast Fibonacci |
| D | Fibonacci Range Sum |
| E | Pattern Prefix Matches |
| F | Suffix LCP Queries |
| G | Domino Placement |
| H | Weighted Tree Distances |
| I | Balanced Subset Difference |
| J | Monge Partition Table |
| K | Online Line DP |
| L | Profitable Disjoint Routes |
| M | Dial Alignment |
| N | Archive Reassembly |
| O | Relay Throughput |
| P | Last Alarm |
| Q | Exact Beacon Codes |
| R | Warehouse Blocks |
| S | Parabolic Signals |

Each package contains its statement, public student stubs, both reference
languages, and tests. All seven new packages include explicit input constraints,
independent small oracles, and maximum-size workloads. The checker runs A--S.

For three shorter rounds, attempt A--F, G--L, then M--S. M--S are grouped by
source topic rather than difficulty. L is an optional extension requiring its
editorial's extra material; leave it aside until the main set is complete.
Use the coverage map in the README only after choosing your own models.

# Diagnose the mathematical object

Before coding, write down what a candidate solution represents. Identify the
allowed choices, the quantity being optimized or counted, and the precise
meaning of one state or maintained object.

```text
What makes a candidate valid?
Which choices interact, and which can be separated?
What changes when I move one endpoint, root, or query position?
What do the largest inputs rule out?
```

Test your proposed model on a tiny case before optimizing it. A repeated value
can expose accidental deduplication; a boundary endpoint can expose an indexing
error; an impossible instance can expose an invalid default answer.

# Proof checkpoints

A reduction needs a mapping in both directions, with the objective preserved.
A recurrence needs an exhaustive description of its last choice. A greedy
choice needs an exchange or dominance argument. An optimization needs its
ordering assumptions proved for the actual cost function, not borrowed from
a similar-looking exercise.

Write those obligations before opening the corresponding source editorial.
The mixed lesson intentionally leaves the individual reductions to your attempt.

# Implementation and testing

Keep public `solve.*` files as stubs and put personal solutions in the private
submissions overlay. The reference checker can be run separately:

```bash
CP_TARGET=solution python3 sections/50_advanced_algorithms_mixed_contest/check.py --keep-going
```

Use independent exhaustive oracles on small inputs. For example, enumerating
all legal choices can check a fast implementation without sharing its internal
state or transition formula. Agreement between two optimized implementations
alone does not establish correctness.

Performance tests serve a separate purpose. A small random case rarely rejects
a quadratic method. M--S each include two full-limit workloads with expected
answers derived from their construction. They run under the normal time limit.
Use wide integers for totals and products, and remember that a valid optimum
can be negative or can count many subsets.

# Exercises

Attempt all eighteen main problems and the optional extension L. For each,
record the model, proof obligation, target complexity, and one counterexample
to a tempting wrong approach. Then use the full editorial to upsolve and
rerun the judge after correcting your implementation.
